# Diagnosing Non-Spelling Radiator Fans on a 1999 Grand Am

When both radiator fans on a 1999 Grand Am refuse to engage after turning on the AC, but you've already ruled out the coolant tank, hoses, temperature sensor, and fuses, the issue almost certainly lies in the control logic rather than the power delivery. The fact that applying direct battery voltage restores fan operation confirms the motors themselves are healthy; they aren't burned out or mechanically seized. This isolates the problem to the circuitry responsible for commanding them to spin.

In this era of General Motors vehicles, the cooling system is managed by a combination of thermal switches and an Engine Control Module (ECM). The ECM acts as the brain, receiving inputs from various sensors and sending ground signals to the fans. Since you have verified the fuses are intact and provided external power that works, we need to trace where the signal path breaks between the sensor input and the fan output.

The most common failure point in a Grand Am of this vintage is the dual-fan relay located under the hood, often near the battery or the strut tower. These relays are electromechanical devices that use a small coil to close heavy-duty contacts for the fan motors. Over time, the internal contacts can carbonize or pitted, preventing them from closing even when the coil receives power. Another frequent culprit is the cooling fan control module (CFM) itself, which sits between the ECM and the fans. If the CFM's internal transistors fail, it will cut off the path to the fans regardless of what the ECM commands.

To systematically diagnose this without guessing, start by checking for voltage at the relay coil terminals when the AC is engaged. Use a multimeter to probe the control side of the relay while the engine is running and the AC compressor is clicking on. If you have 12V at the coil trigger terminal but the fans do not spin, the issue is definitely downstream in the relay or the CFM. If there is no voltage at the trigger terminal, the fault lies upstream in the wiring harness or the ECM.

Another specific weakness in these vehicles involves the thermal switch located on the radiator end tank. While you mentioned replacing the coolant temperature sensor, it is vital to distinguish between the engine coolant temperature (ECT) sensor and the separate thermal fan switches. Many 1999 Grand Ams utilize a bi-metallic thermal switch that closes at specific temperatures (typically around 230Â°F) or when the AC requests cooling. If this specific switch has failed open, the ECM never receives the signal to activate the fans, even if the ECT sensor reports high temperature.

If your diagnostic tools show that the ECM is commanding the fans but the voltage doesn't reach them, the dual-fan relay assembly is likely dead and requires replacement. You can often bypass the CFM or relay temporarily by hard-wiring the fans to a switch fused directly to the battery to confirm they spin with full power, which helps isolate whether the issue is purely electronic control or a more complex wiring fault.

When replacing these components, ensure you check the harness connectors for corrosion or loose pins. A poor connection at the CFM input can mimic a module failure. Also, inspect the ground straps connecting the fan motor assembly to the chassis; a high-resistance ground can prevent the fans from spinning at full speed or stopping them entirely.

If you are working on this vehicle and need reliable replacement parts specifically for GM applications, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes provide access to legacy components or advice on sourcing correct OEM-spec relays and modules. However, always cross-reference part numbers with your specific VIN, as wiring configurations can vary slightly even within the same model year.
